title: Home-Service Call Qualification Flow Builder
note: Spec/data file for the artifact described in ARTIFACT-BRIEF.md. This is structured content only — no HTML/JS is implemented here. Risk descriptions are illustrative consequences of a missing question, never a claim about a real recorded call or about any named vendor's (including Weissmann's) measured behaviour.

service-area.question: What's the postcode, or the street and town?
service-area.whyOrderMatters: Confirmed first, because nothing else is worth establishing if the job is outside the service area.
service-area.riskIfMissing: A technician can be dispatched toward an address before anyone confirms it's within range, wasting the drive and delaying the next genuinely in-area customer.
service-area.riskIfVague: A caller's vague sense of the area ("just outside town") gets treated as confirmed, and the actual distance only becomes clear once a technician is already on the way.

urgency.question: Is water actively running or flowing right now, or has it stopped or slowed?
urgency.whyOrderMatters: Asked early, because it decides whether this call interrupts today's schedule at all, before time goes into details that only matter for an in-scope job.
urgency.riskIfMissing: Two calls both described as "urgent" by tone alone get treated identically, so a routine job can take the one free slot ahead of an active leak.
urgency.riskIfVague: A caller's own word ("bad", "urgent") gets logged without the specific detail a dispatcher needs to compare it against the next call.

job-type.question: In your own words — what's happening, and where (tap, toilet, boiler, pipe, drain)?
job-type.whyOrderMatters: Comes after urgency, so the dispatcher already knows how much time pressure applies before gathering the details.
job-type.riskIfMissing: The technician arrives without knowing which of several different toolkits and parts to bring, and diagnoses the job again from scratch on arrival.
job-type.riskIfVague: A generic description like "a leak" hides whether this is a dripping tap or a burst pipe until someone is standing in the room.

photo.question: Could you send a quick photo or short video of the problem to this number?
photo.whyOrderMatters: Requested once the job type is known, so the caller knows what's useful to photograph.
photo.riskIfMissing: The technician's first real look at the job happens on site, after the van is already loaded on a guess at the right parts.
photo.riskIfVague: A verbal description alone can't show scale, so "a bit of water on the floor" and "water coming through the light fitting" sound similar over the phone and are not.

access.question: Is there anything the technician needs to know to get in — entry code, key location, parking, a pet?
access.whyOrderMatters: Only worth asking once the job is confirmed and scheduled — no point collecting access details for a job that turns out to be out of area.
access.riskIfMissing: A technician arrives on time and then loses fifteen to twenty minutes at the door, eating into the next customer's slot.
access.riskIfVague: An access note like "someone will be around" doesn't say who, or what happens if they're not.

availability.question: When are you actually free for a visit, and will someone be at the address?
availability.whyOrderMatters: Asked last, once every other detail is known, so the window offered is one the business can actually keep.
availability.riskIfMissing: A slot gets promised without checking whether a technician is actually free then, and the office has to call back to walk it back.
availability.riskIfVague: "Anytime" sounds flexible but tells the scheduler nothing usable, so the job defaults to whichever slot is open rather than one that suits the customer.

service-area.question: What's the postcode, or the street and town?
service-area.whyOrderMatters: Confirmed first, for the same reason as any trade: nothing else is worth establishing if the job is outside the service area.
service-area.riskIfMissing: A technician can be sent toward an address before anyone confirms it's within range, wasting the drive and delaying the next genuinely in-area customer.
service-area.riskIfVague: A caller's vague sense of the area gets treated as confirmed, and the real distance only becomes clear once a technician is already on the way.

urgency.question: Is there any smell of burning or visible sparking, or has the power gone out completely — or is this a switch or socket that just isn't working?
urgency.whyOrderMatters: Asked early, for the same reason as any trade: it decides whether the call interrupts today's schedule.
urgency.riskIfMissing: A flickering hallway light and a scorched, sparking socket both get logged as "an electrical problem", so the genuinely dangerous one can wait behind the cosmetic one.
urgency.riskIfVague: "Something's wrong with the wiring" doesn't tell a dispatcher whether this can wait until tomorrow or needs a technician diverted from another job right now.

job-type.question: What exactly isn't working, and where (a single socket, a whole circuit, a light fitting, the fuse box)?
job-type.whyOrderMatters: Comes after urgency, once the time pressure is already established.
job-type.riskIfMissing: The technician can't tell from the booking whether this is a five-minute swap or a fuse-box job, and arrives without the right test equipment.
job-type.riskIfVague: "The electrics are playing up" could mean one loose socket or a failing consumer unit; only one of those is safe to leave until next week.

photo.question: Could you send a photo of the socket, switch or fuse box in question?
photo.whyOrderMatters: Requested once the job type is known, so the caller knows what to photograph.
photo.riskIfMissing: Scorch marks, melted plastic or a tripped breaker that won't reset are all invisible over the phone, and change what the technician should treat as urgent.
photo.riskIfVague: A caller who says "it looks a bit burnt" without a photo leaves the technician guessing how urgent "a bit" really is.

access.question: Is there anything the technician needs to know to get in — entry code, key location, parking, or where the fuse box actually is?
access.whyOrderMatters: Only worth asking once the job is confirmed and scheduled.
access.riskIfMissing: A technician who can get into the building but not find the fuse box loses time that was never accounted for in the slot.
access.riskIfVague: A vague note like "it's somewhere in the basement" leaves the technician searching instead of working.

availability.question: When are you actually free for a visit, and will someone be at the address?
availability.whyOrderMatters: Asked last, once every other detail is known.
availability.riskIfMissing: A slot gets promised without checking technician availability, and the office has to call back to walk it back.
availability.riskIfVague: "Anytime" tells the scheduler nothing usable, so the job defaults to whichever slot is open rather than one that suits the customer.

uiRules.noScoreOrVerdict: This tool must never compute, display or imply a numeric score, percentage, or pass/fail grade — it flags gaps against a fixed question set and shows a suggested order, nothing more.
uiRules.colorRule: Never use colour alone to distinguish the three states — always pair with the text label. No green anywhere; the Weissmann palette has no green.
uiRules.tradeSwitchResets: Switching the trade tab clears the six-row checklist (a plumber's self-assessment does not carry over to the electrician's question set) and shows a brief plain-text notice that it reset.
uiRules.emptyChecklistState: If no row has been marked yet, the Flagged gaps panel shows a neutral prompt, never a false 'no gaps found' message.
uiRules.allClearState: If all six rows are marked 'Asked specifically', show a plain confirmation that no gaps were flagged against this question set, with a one-line reminder that it reflects the reader's own self-assessment, not an independent audit.

disclaimerText: This tool reflects your own self-assessment of your current script, checked against a general good-practice question set — it does not test, record or independently verify any real phone call, and it is not a guarantee of how any specific vendor's system, including Weissmann's, actually performs. The risk descriptions are illustrative consequences of a missing question, not a measured outcome.
privacyNote: The tool runs fully in the browser. There is no field for a real customer's name, address, phone number, or job detail — it only records the reader's own three-state self-assessment per category and reflects it back, without transmitting or requiring it to be saved.
